title: async / await
subtitle: Promise syntax; await yields, resume as microtask

cards.meaning: Syntax over Promises. It does not add a second thread or a new settlement model. It makes async control flow read like synchronous code while still yielding to the event loop at each await.
Always a Promise — even with a plain return, callers get a Promise. A plain return value is wrapped as fulfillment; throw rejects that Promise.
cards.example: async function ok() { return 1; } // Promise fulfilled 1; async function fails() { throw new Error('x'); } // rejected

cards.front: async function returns an existing Promise?
cards.meaning: It adopts/flattens it — same idea as Promise.resolve. Callers still get a Promise that fulfills with the inner value, not Promise<Promise<T>>.
cards.example: async function wrap() { return Promise.resolve(2); } // fulfills with 2

cards.meaning: async function f() {}, const g = async () => {}, object method async m() {}, class method async m() {}.

cards.front: Can a non-async function use await?
cards.meaning: No — only async functions (and modules with top-level await) may use await as a keyword pause point. Using await in a non-async function is a syntax error, except special contexts like some REPL/module top-level cases.

cards.front: Does await block the JavaScript thread?
cards.meaning: No — it pauses the current async function and returns control to the caller / event loop so other code can run. When the awaited Promise settles, the rest of the function is scheduled as a microtask and resumes. It looks synchronous in source, but it never blocks like a busy while loop.

cards.front: log a; f() async with await; log b — order?
cards.meaning: a, f1, b, f2. f() starts and runs sync until await (f1); await suspends f; f() has already returned a Promise to the caller; sync caller continues (b); after the stack clears, microtasks run and f resumes (f2).
cards.example: log a; f(); log b → a, f1, b, f2

cards.meaning: Yes. await x wraps non-Promises roughly like Promise.resolve(x); you still get an async pause/resume (microtask), even for plain values: 1, 3, 2 with surrounding sync logs.
cards.example: async f: log 1; await 0; log 2; f(); log 3 → 1, 3, 2

cards.meaning: Throws at the await expression inside the async function, which rejects the async function's Promise unless caught.
cards.example: async function f() { await Promise.reject(new Error('no')); } f().catch(e => console.log(e.message)); // 'no'

cards.meaning: Each await is a suspension point; the remainder becomes a continuation like .then. That's why readability improves and why native try/catch works across those steps. Desugaring is pedagogical — engines optimize — but the observable model is Promise return + microtask resume.
cards.example: await fetch; await res.json(); return user ≈ fetch().then(res => res.json()).then(user => user)

cards.meaning: Rejections from awaited Promises and synchronous throws in the try body — one control-flow style for sync and async failures in an async function. Multi-step .then/.catch branching gets noisy; this is the ergonomic win.

Handle and recover: catch return fallback. Handle and fail outward: catch log + throw (reject the async function's Promise if the caller must know). Cleanup always: finally. Caller handles: omit catch; let the async Promise reject.

cards.front: If the returned Promise rejects and nobody awaits it?
cards.meaning: Unhandled rejection still applies if nobody awaits or .catch-es it — same rule as the Promises unit.

Accidental serialization when independent — second request starts only after first completes (~2× slower). Rule: if B does not need A's result, do not await A before starting B. Fix: Promise.all([fetchUser(), fetchSettings()]) or start both Promises then await.
Kick off both first, then await: const userP = fetchUser(); const settingsP = fetchSettings(); return { user: await userP, settings: await settingsP }; — or Promise.all as above.

Each fetchItem waits for the previous to finish, so N independent requests take roughly N times longer. Use await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchItem)). If you fear overload, use a concurrency-limited pool — not full serial by default, and not always unbounded parallel.
When each step needs the previous result — cursor pagination, dependent IDs, or rate-limit one-at-a-time by policy.
No. It composes with all / allSettled / race / any — e.g. const settled = await Promise.allSettled([fetchA(), fetchB()]).

1) Run sync code until an await (or function end). 2) At await, schedule resume as a microtask when the awaited Promise settles; continue the caller. 3) After the stack is empty, drain microtasks (resumes, .then, etc.) before the next macrotask.

cards.front: x() with two awaits; logs s1, x(), s2 — order?
cards.meaning: s1, x1, s2, x2, x3. Both resumes are microtasks; no macrotask involved here.
cards.example: async x: log x1; await Promise.resolve(); log x2; await Promise.resolve(); log x3 → s1, x1, s2, x2, x3

cards.front: x() with one await; setTimeout(0); log s?
cards.meaning: x1, s, x2, t — await resume is a microtask before the timer macrotask.
cards.example: setTimeout t; x(); log s → x1, s, x2, t

cards.meaning: Iterates async iterables (objects with Symbol.asyncIterator), awaiting each produced Promise/value. Use when the source is naturally streaming/async.
cards.example: for await (const chunk of asyncStream) { process(chunk); }

cards.meaning: No — iterates Promises, doesn't await them. That does not wait for fetches. Serial: for (const id of ids) await fetchItem(id). Parallel: await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchItem)). for await...of is for async iterables, not a drop-in for an array of Promises.
No — it pulls one at a time from the async iterator. Thinking for await parallelizes is a common mistake.

ES modules in supporting environments/bundlers. Module evaluation waits on that await; importers wait on the module graph. Not available in classic scripts / plain CJS without wrapping. Nest/TS projects: depends on module target and runtime — same caution as the modules unit.
Both return Promises. Prefer async/await when there is branching, multiple steps, or try/catch clarity. Thin wrappers can stay as .then chains.
Usually needless (harmless but noisy) unless you want automatic wrapping of throws. Thin .then chain may suffice.

cards.front: Calling an async function without await/.then?
cards.meaning: Forgetting that async functions return Promises — the caller races ahead. The work is in flight; you didn't wait for it.

cards.front: Does await Promise.all cancel peers on first failure?
cards.meaning: No — same as the Promises unit. It fails fast on the combined Promise only; siblings may still finish unless you abort.
Swallows errors and can return undefined unintentionally. Catch should recover with a fallback, rethrow, or otherwise handle on purpose.

cards.front: Does sync heavy CPU after await still block?
cards.meaning: Yes. Once resumed, that JS still runs on the one thread. Mixing: await yields; then CPU after resume still blocks the thread.

cards.front: Do bindings stay live across await?
cards.meaning: Yes — variables across await points remain the same live bindings. Stale React state in async handlers is still a closure/generation issue, not an await bug.
Start all then Promise.all overlaps host waiting; still one JS thread. Same single-threaded model as the event-loop unit.
Rejection becomes throw at await — same propagation story as .catch, with clearer branches.

Say sugar over Promises and show a mini desugar; prove with log order that await doesn't block the thread; fix sequential dashboard/loop fetches with Promise.all and mention concurrency limits; use try/catch/finally correctly around await; classify when serial await is required vs accidental.
async/await pauses the function and schedules the rest as a microtask when the Promise settles — readable sync style, same single-threaded event loop.
